What he was told, from the judgement: the coercions need no rule about identities, since a sum's zero and a product's one carry into every wider type by themselves while a maximum's identity, the type's least element, does not (both measured); once `where` clauses work, the specification's own identity design (`HasIdentity`, `advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:772-797`) could replace answer 7's witness `typecase` for `SUM`'s zero and `PROD`'s one without changing what a program gets, and `MAX` and `MIN` still get no identity on the integers or floats. One ledger note records it.
114	- 2026-09-26, rung D's stop in climb batch 5 (one interpreter test, `XXXInheritedOverload.fss`, names its two ambiguous overloads in the other order, as the untouched tree already does from run to run): "Okay, so it just sounds like we had a rule too stringent because the spirit of the test is still held. We just discovered a flaky test and this didn't need to be raised up to me. And the other issues from RunD entered the ledger for a review. So yeah, of course, uh, do the A. Push it. Commit and push it. We are not holding this." D landed as a follow-up to batch 5 (`ab914b6e0`). For every brief since: an output difference that the untouched tree already shows from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is not a stop; it is a ledger row (here row 430, provisionally 406). A rung's small items go to the ledger for review, not to him one per message.
115	- 2026-09-26, on the record's rule that a message sent while the coordinator is mid-turn kills a running batch: "This is probably like edge case that we encountered only once, or even there we might have misinterpreted that I accidentally pressed stop button and the diagnosis was wrong? Maybe this is a work for an archaeology worker (Sonnet for digging but Opus for final analysis/judgement?) so that we do not cargo cult around non-existent problem." The archaeology (`coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/`) found that stopping a turn kills the background agents and a message kills nothing (FACTS § The container); the error was the coordinator's. The rule for him now, which he has been told: send messages at any time; do not press stop while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; if a stop happens by accident, say so and the batch is relaunched.
116	- 2026-09-26, rung S's stop on the calculi of Appendix A (`compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` § 4.2, three options): "Agreed." to option 1 — Core Fortress with Where Clauses, ACFFD and Basic Core each carry a `\revision` callout saying that the calculus predates instantiation exclusion and admits the shapes the rule refuses, with their rules and soundness claims untouched, and Appendix I's entry "The calculi" replaces its "not yet revised" wording for them. Built (`eb2d7e1e6`).
117	- 2026-09-26, the launch of climb batch 6: "Once Fable's feedback is incorporated into the batch manifest and there are no questions for me, you are also approved to launch the next workflow batch." A conditional go: the coordinator launches batch 6 without asking again when the Fable review of `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` is folded in and the manifest's section for Pavol holds no open question; if any question for him remains, it goes to him first, one per message, and the launch waits for his answers.
118	- 2026-09-26, Q1 of batch 6 (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` section 1: team test lines the flat tower breaks beyond the approved ones, `Generator2Test`, `setSum`, `asifTest:102` and whatever rung F's comparison finds): "A". Rung F respells each such line keeping the value the test checks, deletes no assertion, and lists every line for him with its before and after. With no question left, his conditional go (the entry on the launch of climb batch 6) takes effect and the coordinator launches the batch.
119	- 2026-09-26, 23:59 UTC, asked what he could pre-approve so that rung O's follow-up also runs overnight (its launch was already part of batch 6's go; it starts only from a landed and pushed batch 6): "Yes" to lifting one of rung T's stops in advance. A passage of the specification whose new text neither his decisions nor rung F's coercion table settle (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` section 3, T, "Stops") is left as it stands, named in Appendix I as not yet revised, as the calculi were until his answer, and listed for him afterwards; it does not hold batch 6's push. It costs one small follow-up later that writes those passages. Every other stop reserved for him still holds the push.
120	
121	## How he wants to be spoken to
122	
123	- The register. 2026-09-15: "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations. 2026-09-19: "this is a wall of text that I cannot absorb"; "you were writing in the smart aleck register. If you wrote it in plain English, that would be helpful. But I still don't understand what decisions are we taking and what are the impacts." 2026-09-20: replies very brief, plain English, no internal jargon. 2026-09-21: "It borders on the smart Alec essayist register. It is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." So: plain register, short sentences; label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication).
124	- A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
125	- He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; an inventory of what is running answers "is anything in flight" from the tree, not from the UI.
126	- Asks and decisions. 2026-09-19: decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat. 2026-09-21, after three turns in which the coordinator asked for yeses on named items ("decision F", "the stage", "the base") without saying what the work would do: "What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? We have rules in place that ask for my permissions. I want to move the work forward and I want to say yes. But this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding." An ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs; one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
127	- 2026-09-19: the harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently — "I don't really need to hear about those reminders at all"; while work is in flight they are declined without a word, and they are never mentioned to him.
128	- 2026-09-20, after the compaction that closed a session he called "an absolute disaster" — he "felt out of control, unaware of crucial details", and the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts": the coordinator's standing goal is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected.
129	- 2026-09-20, while a batch runs: he wants no progress reports on it until it lands. He asked then for the time of every scheduled check-in, so that he could avoid sending a message during that turn; a message sent during a turn is queued and kills nothing (the entry of 2026-09-26 on the interrupt archaeology), so whether he still wants the check-in times is his to say. He is on Central European time; check-in times are given to him in UTC and in his local time.
130	- 2026-09-22, on format: "table formatted in this way is hard to read on mobile … we just need a list" — no tables in chat; lists. On the re-approval review's purpose: "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival" — every row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. The array decisions (A: the mechanism that puts `double[]` under a float vector; B: where unboxed arithmetic happens; D: sizes in the model's own types) stay after the switch-over, with plain explainers prepared beforehand. And for the cleaner pass later: GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches (he was cut off mid-sentence; the rest is held).
131	- 2026-09-23, on numbers in chat: "write the numbers just as K or M. I'm fine as a programmer understanding what a kilo is" — never spelled-out thousands and millions; and a message dense with numbers is one he "heard all the words, understood almost nothing" of, so a numbers message carries few numbers, each with its meaning. On the coordinator's two hats: "executive assistant here in this Fortress Revival project, helping me, the director, find a way forward, and the analyst that finds out what the fuck happened, why, and how do we move forward".
132	- 2026-09-23, on time in chat: talking about time is fine when it is read from the clock or the record, when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires. What is forbidden is the casual placement of events in time from feel, "yesterday", "this morning", "last night", when they were minutes or hours apart; in the coordinator's prose "time flows like if you were on a rocket at light speed". Protocol § 3.
133

content.text: Most dropped text is either still in POSITIONS.md in shorter form or was a one-off. Now the batch workflow manual, where the manifest-review method and the gate details should be.

content.content:
1	<!-- What `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` does stage by stage after the 2026-09-19 generalisation, and
2	     which review item each change answers. The decisions are `coordinator/process-decisions-review-1.md`
3	     as amended and `POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-19 ("after climb batch 1 landed"); the eight free changes are
4	     `repair-batch-review.md` section 10. Item numbers below are those two lists. -->
5	
6	# The batch workflow script, stage by stage
7	
8	The script runs *a* batch, not batch 1. Everything a batch changes lies between the `MANIFEST` and `END MANIFEST` markers: the batch number, its decision record, its intro and overlap sentences, the first free ledger row, and one entry per rung — `id`, `slug`, `path`, `branch`, `tail`, `blurb`, `expectedMinutes`, `writesState`, `expectedMoves`, the three optional fields of the checker-count stage, `testIsStage`, `expectedCheckerCount` and `expectedCheckerCrash`, and the optional `landsOnlyWith` (below). Batch 1's manifest is left in place as the example.
9	
10	## Manifest and scatter (item 8)
11	
12	`expectedMinutes` sorts the scatter, longest-expected worker first: 0–12 minutes when the guess is right, free when it is not. k stays 4. The two-agent cap and the FIFO handing of a freed slot to the next queued agent are a comment on the manifest block with their `FACTS.md` sources; rung chains (decision 2(a)) are not implemented and the comment says why — replayed on batch 1's walls they save 0.3 minutes. Ledger numbering follows manifest order, not scatter order, and the script maps the results back.
13	
14	`landsOnlyWith`, added 2026-09-26 for batch 6 (`CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` section 8, item 4), is a list of rung ids a rung lands only with: batch 6's T, the number chapters, names F, the flat library they describe. After the scatter, and before anything is handed on, `applyLandsOnlyWith` withholds every approved rung any of whose named rungs is not approved (stopped, dropped, its worker dead, withheld itself, or absent from the run), and repeats until nothing moves. A withheld rung keeps its approval in `approvedAs`, takes the state `withheld` and a `withheldReason` naming the rung it waited for and that rung's state, and reaches the gather on the not-landed list, so its source is never applied and its findings are folded as for any rung that did not land; its `expectedMoves` and checker declarations no longer count at the gate. Until then such a rule lived in the batch intro alone, which only the gather's reading enforced (batch 5's rule for rung Z's `cP` piece; `climb-batch-6-review.md`, change 10). A rung that is not in the run cannot be approved, so an entry that names one is withheld: batch 6's O names F only when it runs beside F (`FOLLOWUP ? [] : ['F']`).
15	
16	
17	## Preparing a batch record
18	
19	An Opus planning worker drafts `CLIMB-BATCH-<n>.md` and commits it. On Pavol's yes each time, one Fable worker then reviews it in place: it edits the record directly, writes one reason per change in a short review note (`climb-batch-6-review.md` is the example), and commits, so that the diff between the two versions shows exactly what the review changed. The coordinator reads that diff, fixes what is left, and brings the questions in section 1 to Pavol one per message; the batch launches on his go (batches 5 and 6; his words in the two entries of 2026-09-26 on the review of those manifests, `git show e5414f5bf:explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, lines 150 and 171).
20	
21	## Shared prefix
22	
23	New: a `run_bg`/`wait_for` pair at five-second granularity (item 7); a committed capture is `.txt`, never `.out` or `.log` (`.gitignore:42,46`, item h); `ant` is never piped through `tail` (item i). Rule 2 asks for the site count when a precedent repaired a defect (item 6); rule 3 asks for the passage rather than the grep hit, ten lines either side (item 2). Rule 4's closing sentence, and the judge's `stop` question with it, named batch 3.5's two stops, a change to a declared type the prelude already has and a renamed or removed declaration a gated test uses, as if they applied to every batch; since 2026-09-26 both point to the stops the batch record's intro reserves for Pavol, at the head of the prefix (`open-items-2026-09-26.md`, item 27; batch 6's rung F changes declared types by Pavol's decisions). The register paragraph limits a test file to one comment line pointing at its `REPORT.md` (item e, `protocol.md` section 2).
24	
25	"What a measured defect is worth" is the rule that closes the 22-and-2 gap. Every defect anyone measures has one of three homes and the record says which:
26	
27	1. **repaired in the rung**, whoever measured it → an assertion in the rung's own gated test, passing before the second skeptic runs (item a);
28	2. **deferred, specification settles it** → a gated expected-failure test named `XXX…` asserting the specification's answer. The mechanism is cited so it can be checked: `FileTests.java:932` sets `shouldFail` from the name and `:587`/`:654` make `shouldFail != failed` the failure condition, so the suite goes red the day the test starts passing; `:851` names the case and the author's warning at `:853` is why a rung's first `XXX` file is shown to go red on a deliberate local fix (item b);
29	3. **deferred, specification silent** → a probe with a committed `.txt` capture and a ledger row, the record saying the silence is the reason (item c).
30	
31	The tracked-path check is here too: every `explorations/` path a record cites is `git ls-files --error-unmatch`'d before the rung reports (item g, gap 4).
32	
33	## Rung worker
34	
35	Step 1 fixes the check line at `run_out_contains=PASS` and notes that `run_out_WIcontains` is now implemented rather than silently inert (item d). Step 8 is the three-homes obligation. The provenance block gains a fifth line, `historical:`, naming every 2012-tree file the rung edits (item 8, `protocol.md:126-127`). Step 11 is the tracked-path check. `RUNG_SCHEMA` gains `historicalFiles`, `defectHomes`, `trackedPaths`.
36	
37	Since 2026-09-26 it also carries `reportText` and `recordText`, the full text of `REPORT.md` and `record.md` word for word, and `stopsMet`, which is required. In batch 5 the harness refused the rung workers' writes of `REPORT.md`, and the gather composed each report from the structured result, whose `summary` is at most 15 lines (`CLIMB-BATCH-6.md` section 8, item 1). `stopsMet` lists every stop the batch record's intro reserves for Pavol that the rung met, including one met on part of the work while the rest lands. Each entry has the stop, its evidence and `liftedBy`, which is the `POSITIONS.md` line of the decision of Pavol's that lifts it, or empty. The skeptic and the merged-diff review return the same field (`STOPS_MET`), and the commit stage reads all three (below).
38	
39	Each rung's worker commits and pushes to its own `wip/<slug>` branch as it works, so a dead container loses nothing; the gather composes one commit per rung on `main`.
40	
41	## Skeptic
42	
43	Check 7 is the three homes — the skeptic runs the test itself to see a home-1 assertion pass. Check 0 covers the fifth provenance line. A rung whose manifest entry sets `writesState` has every differential run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` **and** `=4`, both columns reported (item f, gap 2); a rung without it is told to do the same if its reading of the diff finds a mutable variable, a field, an `atomic` block or a write into `CompilerLibrary`'s state. `SKEPTIC_SCHEMA` gains `recommendedRows` (item 1), `threadCounts`, `defectHomes`, and since 2026-09-26 `skepticText` (the text of `SKEPTIC.md`) and a required `stopsMet`, in which the skeptic names every reserved stop the rung meets as it stands, whether or not the worker named it; its approval lifts none.
44	
45	Check 8, added 2026-09-23, compares the rung's own count table with its report; it is a file read and runs nothing. The skeptic takes `#total` from the committed post-edit table the brief names (`probes/checker-count-postedit.txt` for a `testIsStage` rung) and compares it with the total the report declares. A mismatch goes into `requiredCorrections` with both numbers, so the report is corrected and the rung does not stop over it. A rung that declares a count, in its report or as `expectedCheckerCount`, with no table path named gets the finding "no count table"; a rung that declares none has nothing to compare. The manifest's `expectedCheckerCount` is written beside the two as a prediction, not a value the table must meet. This is f1 of `climb-batch-3-redesign.md` § 4, which `checker-gate-review.md` § 4 recommends taking with the report-only gate: in batch 3 nothing set L's committed table (103) beside the declared 102 between 19:14 and the gate at 00:43.
46	
47	A judge's first ruling on a rung or on the merged tree runs on Opus; a second ruling on the same rung or tree runs on Fable (`judgeTier`; POSITIONS 2026-09-26).
48	
49	## Gather
50	
51	Rungs are applied in ascending order of lowest edited line in the shared files, and a cited `file:line` that an earlier applied rung shifted is re-anchored by symbol (item 5). Each `recommendedRows` entry is opened or refused in one sentence (item 1). After a rung's patch is applied, each of its `REPORT.md`, `record.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` that the branch does not carry is written from `reportText`, `recordText` and `skepticText` verbatim (with a first skeptic round's text under "## First round" where there were two); a file the branch carries stands. The same holds for a rung that did not land, whose files are taken out of its branch. Files are staged by an explicit list and `git diff --cached --stat` is read before the commit, never `git add` of a directory (`protocol.md` section 4, 2026-09-19). A commit touching any path outside `explorations/` carries a `historical:` line (item 8, 7c). A rung that stopped, was dropped or was withheld by `landsOnlyWith` has its `SKEPTIC.md` findings, its recommended rows and the probes those findings cite — taken out of its branch path by path — folded under a "Not landed" heading with no source applied (7a, gap 3). After the last commit the tracked-path check runs over every landed record (7b).
52	
53	## Review beside the gate
54	
55	Both run in one `parallel()` — the substitute the review recommended for the rejected rung chains, 14.7 minutes per batch off the serial tail. The risk of two agents committing at once is closed by the gate committing nothing; the commit stage adds its summary. The review records the head before and after its corrections commit, runs `git diff --name-only` between them, and returns every path outside `explorations/`; a non-empty list re-runs the gate, and so does a blocking finding that goes to the judge. Check 10, added 2026-09-26, lists in `stopsMet` every reserved stop a landed rung meets, in its hunks or where its records say so; it is not a blocking finding, and the commit stage reads it.
56	
57	## Gate
58	
59	Disk, `compileAll`, the library rebuild **plus a copy of the fresh library cache** for the ladder stage, `testFast`, `testSystem`, the summary and its comparison, the four-thread `atomic` runs, the ladder regression, and since 2026-09-22 the checker count, which has its own section below. Logs go to `tmp/gate-batch-<N>/`, which `.gitignore:64` now ignores (appended at the end of the file so that no existing `.gitignore` citation moves), never committed. The `"Tests expected to pass are failing"` grep is gone (item 4): it is ant's own `<fail message=…>` and reads the same dial as `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`.
60	
61	`summary.txt` comes from a fixed shell snippet in the script, not agent prose (item 3): one row per suite — `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped — read from the plain-formatter files under `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-*/` and `system-*/`, because the four parallel `testFast` tracks interleave their `Running` and `Tests run:` lines in the ant log and cannot be paired there; the `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` and `Total time` lines come from the logs. `gate_compare` diffs it against the newest landed summary, found with `git log --name-only`; a suite whose count fell, or that is gone, is red and named (gap 1). The `system-<i>` rows are compared by their sum, not one by one: `testSystem` is one suite sharded by sorted index (`FileTests.java:790-806`), so a file added to `ProjectFortress/tests/` moves every later file along the shards; climb batch 2's gate went red on exactly this after `02d09a39f` added two interpreter tests between the baseline and the batch base (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md`). `run_bg` runs its command string in a subshell so a `cd` inside it cannot escape the log, and `atomic_runs` resolves its out-file before its own `cd` (both measured by that batch's gate stage). The first landed summary is `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/summary.txt`.
62	
63	The four-thread stage runs the thirteen `atomic` programs the repair batch measured — the ten of `other_compiler_tests/atomicTest.test` plus `AtomicTopLevelObjectVar`, `AtomicTopLevelVar` and `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop` — three times each at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`. Any `FAIL`, `NO-PASS` or compile failure is red; a timeout is re-run once and then red. The 39 lines go into the summary.
64	
65	The ladder stage re-runs the 85 files of `baseline-2026-09-19/pass-list.txt` and the eighteen microGPT components of `microgpt-phase.md` with the baseline's own drivers, copying the gate's fresh library cache instead of rebuilding one. The 85 are compared on phase **and** stdout, with a filter masking the `Operation took …ms` line: those three `nestedTransactions` captures are the only ones of the 85 whose output varies, and masking the line rather than exempting the file keeps the rest of their output checked. The eighteen are **compiled only** — `fortress compile`, the phase reached — never linked and never run in this stage (Pavol, 2026-09-19); when they one day compile, running them is a separate non-gating stage, not the gate. A `DOWN`, `STDOUT` or `MISSING` line is red unless `expectedMoves` declared it; a move up is the batch's result and is reported. The judge's `gate` question now names the ways the gate can be red — five since the checker count below — and where each one's evidence is.
66	
67	## The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage (2026-09-22)
68	
69	The gate's eighth step runs the compiler's static checker over the **interpreter's** library and compares its error total with the last landed one. It answers Pavol's decision of 2026-09-21 (`POSITIONS.md`, "the library route"): one library, the interpreter's `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the library the compiler checks, and the compiler's own prelude is deleted at the switch-over. Step 1 of `library-route-judgement.md` is what makes the distance a stage rather than a script — it was measured twice by hand (92 on 2026-09-16, 93 on 2026-09-19) and nothing kept it measured, which is the one-off validation these rules forbid everywhere else. Pavol's own objection is on record and this stage does not answer it: a count is a metric, not a measure of the work behind it (`postmortem-2026-09-19/positions-checker-gate.md`, 15:18).
70	
71	The stage is `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`, with `WorldFlip.java` and the instrumented `StaticChecker` copy beside it — both copied from `perf-probes/prelude/`, so that the gate does not depend on a probe directory. It compiles the two against `bin/fortress_classpath`, puts the shadow checker ahead of `ProjectFortress/build`, and runs the compiler phase order over `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` with `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()` under its own `-Dfortress.caches` in the gate's log directory: no library rebuild, nothing written into `default_repository/`, 20 s. Its table is one row per api with that api's error count, then `#total`, `#locations` (the distinct `file:line` the errors were reported at), `#crash` (the crash the checker meets after the apis — today the `nat` gap, `Not yet implemented` at `STypesUtil.scala:557`) and `#shadow`, which says whether the copy still matches the tracked checker, because a copy of a tracked source goes stale silently and then the number is not this tree's. `checker_compare` is red on a total that rose, on a changed crash line and on a stale shadow, each unless a rung of the batch declared it in `expectedCheckerCount` or `expectedCheckerCrash`; a total that fell is the batch's result and is reported, and the per-api rows and `#locations` are printed either way and are not themselves red. `last_landed_checker_count` finds the comparand the way `last_landed_summary` finds the summary, over `gate-baseline/checker-count.txt` and `climb-batch-*/gate/checker-count.txt`; the gate writes the table and commits nothing, and the commit stage lands it beside `summary.txt`, which is what keeps the chain of comparands unbroken. The first comparand is `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/checker-count.txt`, this change's own dry run on the tree at `6a6b36531`.
72	
73	Until 2026-09-23 that comparison was a gate: a total above the last landed one was red unless it equalled a rung's `expectedCheckerCount`, and in climb batch 3 it went red on L's 103 against a declared 102. Since then the total is reported and is never red on its own, for the reasons in `checker-gate-review.md` (§ 2, and § 4, which recommends option (b) with (f)'s stale-copy check): a fix can raise the count, because the checker stops checking an api at its first errors (`StaticChecker.java:268-272`), and two rungs' changes do not add, so neither a rise nor a missed declaration tells progress from harm. `checker_compare` prints `COUNT UP`, `COUNT DOWN` or `COUNT SAME` with the last landed total, the measured one and the declared totals, as in `COUNT UP   93 -> 103, declared L: 102`, and exits 1 only on a crash line no rung declared, a stale shadow or a table with no total. Dry-run over the landed baseline and batch-3 tables, the rise exits 0 with or without a declaration, and a stale shadow or an undeclared crash change exits 1. `expectedCheckerCount` stays in the manifest as a prediction the gate prints. Explaining the change is now the merged-diff review's job: its check 9 waits for the gate's table (the `#shadow` row is written last), diffs it against the last landed one, and ties every new or risen row to a named rung edit, one line each in a new `checkerRows` field; a row it cannot tie to a rung edit is blocking and goes to the judge and a repair. The judge's `gate` question and the rung and skeptic briefs no longer say an undeclared rise is red. Two sentences still say the count may only fall and are left for their own edits: the header of `run.sh` and the manifest comment on `expectedCheckerCount`, which the next manifest replaces.
74	
75	A rung whose manifest entry sets `testIsStage` has that stage as its test. Step 1 of the order of work then asks for the stage's table captured before the edit and step 2 for the table after it, in place of the `.fss` component and its `.test` file; the skeptic's check 1 asks for both captures and re-runs the stage itself to see the second one come out again, and check 4 checks the two tables differ in the way the report says. Nothing else about such a rung changes — the ladder subset, the three homes, the provenance block and the tracked-path check all stand. - **The Workflow harness runs two agents at once on this box** (measured 2026-09-18, four one-command agents in one `parallel()`: agents 0 and 1 started 19:14:08, agents 2 and 3 at 19:14:31 after the first pair finished at 19:14:23; `batched-climb-plan.md` §2). `model: 'opus'` in `agent()` resolves to a fixed model identifier, readable in each agent transcript's `message.model` field and not written here (protocol §4); an agent with no `model` inherits the session's. A subagent's floor is about 45k tokens before it does anything (183k for the four). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (33,022 tokens read by agents 1–3) and not the first user message (11,010 written by each), because a cache read lands only at a breakpoint the harness placed and a shared prefix inside one message is not one.
- The VM can be restarted under a live session with the disk intact: 2026-09-18 23:22 UTC, 25 minutes into the repair batch's re-run, kernel build string fc-v33 → fc-v37, one JVM running (16 GB, no swap, 4 CPUs: not a memory death). Worktrees, uncommitted edits and agent transcripts survived; the Workflow run and its agents did not, and a run is relaunched, never resumed; the `wip/` branches held every pushed milestone (`remote-container.md` § The 2026-09-18 restart).
- **A user interrupt of the coordinating session's turn kills a background Workflow run** (2026-09-19): climb batch 1's first run, `wf_a29fd04b-a9a`, launched 07:15 UTC, lost both its rung agents at 07:46:42, the second Pavol's interrupt cut the turn that a check-in trigger had just started; both agent transcripts end at that timestamp mid-work, no result line reached the journal, and the harness no longer knew the task. The Agent tool's workers are not affected (the review worker launched after the interrupt ran to completion). The `wip/` branches held F's three and M's three milestones and M's worktree its uncommitted report, so the relaunch at 08:25 from the same base continued under the prefix's continuation clause. Cost: about 40 minutes of two workers. Rule: while a Workflow runs, a check-in must not be interrupted mid-turn; and a batch is relaunched, never resumed, after any such death. Corrected 2026-09-26: this entry said "the Agent tool's workers are not affected"; a background `Agent`-tool worker alive at an interrupt dies with it at the same instant (two at 2026-09-22 07:18:51, one at 2026-09-25 22:31:59 after a stop Pavol reported pressing by accident), and the review worker cited was launched after the interrupt, so it tested nothing; no message caused this death (none was enqueued between the check-in at 07:46:30 and Pavol's next message at 07:48:34, and at 09:05 he said he had pressed nothing); rung F had written its closing text at 07:45:41 without returning its result, so only M was mid-work; the rule covers every turn, not only a check-in (session `fe616d40`, main transcript and `subagents/`).
- **A message from Pavol that arrives while the coordinator is inside a turn kills a running Workflow's agents, whatever the turn is doing** (2026-09-26, batch 5, run `wf_eb47c103-304`, launched 11:10 UTC). At 12:07:47 UTC his message interrupted a turn that was recording a decision, not a check-in. Both rung agents' transcripts end at that second with "[Request interrupted by user for tool use]", the journal stops at their two `started` lines, and the harness no longer knows the task (`TaskStop` finds no such task). What survived: rung Z's three pushed commits and rung D's one, with their worktrees' uncommitted files, and rung D's orphaned count run. The coordinator's own advice at the launch, that messages between check-ins are safe, was wrong: a message is safe only while the coordinator is idle, between turns. Same mechanism as the entry above of 2026-09-19. Corrected 2026-09-26: no message caused this death; it was an interrupt, as on 09-19: the turn's pending Bash is recorded "User rejected tool use" at 12:07:47.797 and "[Request interrupted by user]" at .799, and no message was enqueued between "Yes, agreed." (12:07:33, already delivered) and the next one at 12:08:32; at 12:09 Pavol asked whether he had pressed stop by accident and at 12:10 named the iOS stop button under his right thumb. A message sent during a turn is queued, not an interrupt: it is delivered inside the turn (16:13:08 the same day, with `wf_88172730-ebe` working on) or as the next turn, and eleven such messages during live runs from 09-19 to 09-26 killed none. The launch advice that messages are safe was right; this entry's headline, "his message interrupted a turn" and "a message is safe only while the coordinator is idle" are wrong (session `fe616d40`, main transcript 12:07:33-12:10:46 and 16:13:08; `subagents/workflows/wf_eb47c103-304/`).
- **A manual compaction issued between turns leaves a running Workflow alive** (found 2026-09-19 by a worker in the archived transcript of session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, parts file `001.jsonl`): the eight-rung climb's run `wf_73833dfb-d25` (launched 2026-09-17 06:00:57 UTC) survived two `/compact` commands, boundaries 10:47:33 (442,504 tokens before, 130 s) and 14:25:25 (177,831 tokens, 153 s), both typed while the session sat between turns; rung 5's commit landed 84 s after the first boundary, rungs 6-8 and the final re-run followed, and the run's completion notification arrived 14:39:09 with all eight rungs. This container's three compactions (09-18 18:38, 22:54; 09-19 06:38) coincided with no run. So the rule is: compact between turns, never send during a turn; the 09-19 death was a mid-turn interrupt, not a compaction. Caveat: that run's journal and agent transcripts are not in the backup, so the agents' survival is inferred from their commits and the session's own status turns. Corrected 2026-09-26: "never send during a turn" is wrong, since a message sent during a turn is queued and kills nothing (the entry above, corrected); and the caveat is closed: three manual compactions in this container fell inside live runs, 09-19 09:47 (`wf_3b5a273c-a80`), 09-20 05:32 (`wf_d1628adb-2ee`) and 09-26 12:26 (`wf_88172730-ebe`), and each run's agents kept writing through the compaction (40 to 66 records inside its window) and went on to their results (session `fe616d40`, `subagents/workflows/`).
- **Stopping a turn kills every background agent alive at that moment; a message sent while the coordinator is busy kills nothing** (2026-09-26, `coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/judgement.md` § 1, from `coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/evidence.md`; session `fe616d40`, main transcript, `subagents/` and `subagents/workflows/`; session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, `001.jsonl`). The kill is the turn interrupt the transcript records as "[Request interrupted by user]", with any tool still in flight recorded "User rejected tool use": in the four interrupts that met live background agents (2026-09-19 07:46:42, 09-22 07:18:51, 09-25 22:31:59, 09-26 12:07:47) all seven agents alive died at that instant, Workflow agents and `Agent`-tool workers alike, and none ever survived one. Eleven messages and three `/context` commands sent while the coordinator was busy, during five live runs from 09-19 to 09-26, killed nothing: each was queued and delivered inside the running turn or as the next turn. Five manual compactions between turns killed nothing either (09-17 10:47 and 14:25, 09-19 09:47, 09-20 05:32, 09-26 12:26). That the stop button sent the interrupt is confirmed for 09-25 in Pavol's words and very likely for 09-26 (the iOS client's stop control under his right thumb), not shown for 09-19; the transcripts record the effect, not the control. Not tested: an automatic compaction mid-turn, and an interrupt during the Stop hook while a run is alive. The rule: send messages at any time; compact between turns; do not stop a turn while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; after an accidental stop, say so and the batch is relaunched (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the interrupt ruling). The three entries above carry the corrections.
- **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` is the one script every probe and gate runner sources, and it is verified from its new home** (2026-09-24, after `7bc8177a3` moved `experiment/` under `explorations/`): it derives `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own location two levels up, and re-running the two shadow experiments that source it, `reviews/mie-probes/forest/forest-run.sh` (423 s) and `perf-probes/nat/runtime/run-all.sh` (669 s), reproduced every committed count and probe output (`checker-count.txt`'s six counts, stock 103 and forest 37 among them, and captures r1-r5 byte-identical); the only differences were dates, timings and line numbers shifted by the library commits `c2b4e2c95` and `d6faad28f` made after the captures. astra's scripts keep their own `experiment/` paths, which name astra's tree.
- **A check-in cadence under an hour is a series of one-shot `send_later` check-ins armed together in one turn, not a cron trigger and not a re-armed one-shot** (2026-09-26, a Sonnet worker's search of session `fe616d40`'s main transcript at Pavol's request). The scheduler's cron triggers take an hour as their shortest interval. For batch 5, at 11:10:40-43 UTC, the coordinator made seven `send_later` calls in one turn, each `{"at": ..., "name": "Batch 5 check-in N", "message": ...}`, `at` 12:40 to 17:10 UTC 45 minutes apart; they fired at 12:40:47, 13:25:43, 14:10:41, 14:55:50, 15:40:28, 16:25:54 and 17:10:58, within a minute of each target, with no re-arming. Batch 4's four were 90 minutes apart (01:31 UTC, `at` 03:01 to 07:31), though one of them was relabelled "one of the 45-minute series". Batches 1 to 3 chained one `send_later` per check-in, each re-issued by the turn it started (batch 3 fired seven times at 58-60 minute spacing). The scheduler refuses more than about ten trigger creations a minute: the eleventh `send_later` of batch 6's series, at 23:50:52 UTC, got "Trigger creation rate limit reached. Try again in 56s." A series ends when its last check-in has fired, so a run that outlasts it needs a new series, armed by the last check-in.

## The ledger

=====
snapshot writes whole files with no delta, so the object store grows by tens of
megabytes per commit: 21.3 GiB of loose objects by 2026-09-17, which packed down
to 609 MB. `backup.sh` now ends with `git -c gc.auto=1000 gc --auto`. Unrelated
but same symptom: the Rats! temp directories in `FACTS.md` § The container.

**Worktree state that is never committed.** The first repair batch forbade its
workers to commit, so that the gather could compose one clean commit per rung;
when the container died every worktree was dirty and four agents' work went
with it. The transcript backup does not cover this: it copies JSONL, not trees,
and it fires only at the main session's Stop. The fix is in the workflow design
(`batched-climb-plan.md` §3, revised 2026-09-18): each worker's worktree is on
its own `wip/<slug>` branch, pushed at every milestone, and the gather composes
from the branch's net change instead of the dirty tree. Two rules follow for
any long run: nothing that takes hours lives only on disk, and the coordinator
takes a turn every half hour or so (`send_later`) so that the Stop hook fires
and the agents' transcripts are snapshotted while they run.

## Setting up a batch's worktrees

The workflow script cannot touch the filesystem before its first agent runs, so
the coordinator creates the worktrees and pushes the empty branches first, from
the commit `main` is at, which is then the script's `args.base`:

```sh
cd /home/user/fortress && BASE=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
for r in r1-atomic-static r2-literal-wrap; do
  git worktree add -b wip/repair-$r /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*} main
  cp -a ProjectFortress/build /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/ProjectFortress/   # javac incremental; scalac rebuilds anyway
  mkdir -p /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/tmp
  git push -u origin wip/repair-$r
done

Lost: the four workflow agents (`rung:R1`, `rung:R2`, `skeptic:R1`,
`skeptic:R2`, ~798k tokens), their isolated worktrees, and the 13 hours after
the last snapshot. Not lost: everything committed through `2ab1d6d8`, the
workflow script, `REPAIR-BATCH.md` — written the same afternoon *"for a session
that was not present"*, which is why the batch remains runnable — and the
conversation through 20:31.

Recovery was carried out in the blinded run's container, which already had the
checkout and the toolchain: fast-forward to `main`, fix the backup, materialise
the other lineage's transcripts, then re-run the batch from its recorded brief.

## The 2026-09-19 interrupt

A Workflow run lives inside the coordinating session's turn structure even though
it is reported as a background task: when Pavol interrupted the session's turn at
07:46:42 UTC, eleven seconds after a scheduled check-in had started it, both rung
agents of climb batch 1 stopped at that second and the harness forgot the task
(`TaskGet` returned not found). An `Agent`-tool worker launched afterwards was
unaffected. Recovery was the same as after the VM restart: the `wip/` branches
and the worktrees held everything pushed and everything on disk, and the batch
was relaunched from the same base with the same command. Two consequences: a
check-in that fires during a batch should be left to finish its turn, and a
Workflow run is never resumed after such a death, only relaunched.

A compaction is not an interrupt. The eight-rung climb of 2026-09-17 (run
`wf_73833dfb-d25`) ran through two manual `/compact` commands, at 10:47 and 14:25
UTC, both issued between turns, and completed at 14:39 with all eight rungs;
the evidence is the session's archived transcript (`bdff267d`, parts file
`001.jsonl`: the compact boundaries, the first post-compaction turn declining to
commit "the running workflow's rung 5", and the completion notification). So
while a batch runs: compact freely between turns; do not send while a turn is
in flight.

*Corrected 2026-09-26:* the interrupt is not a message. What stops a turn, and
every background agent with it, Workflow agents and background `Agent`-tool
workers alike (two workers at 2026-09-22 07:18:51, one at 2026-09-25 22:31:59), is
the interrupt the transcript records as "[Request interrupted by user]"; on
2026-09-26 at 12:07:47 it was very likely the iOS stop button. A message sent
while a turn is in flight is queued, delivered inside the turn or as the next
turn, and in eleven cases from 09-19 to 09-26 it cut no turn and killed no run. So
while a batch runs: send whenever; compact between turns; do not press stop in any
turn, not only a check-in.

## The 2026-09-18 restart

The repair batch's re-run was launched at 22:57 UTC (run `wf_9777a563-c5e`,
session `fe616d40-…`). At about 23:22, 25 minutes in, the VM was restarted:
the two agents' last records are 23:22:20 and 23:22:23, a test's output file
was still being written at 23:22:29, and `uptime` read 0 minutes at 23:23:29
on a kernel whose build string had changed (fc-v33 to fc-v37). One JVM was
running across both worktrees at that moment, on 16 GB with no swap, so the
load was not the cause; a platform restart is the only reading the record
supports.

What it cost: the two rung agents' working context, 25 minutes of two workers.
What it did not cost: the disk survived, so the worktrees, their uncommitted
edits, their `tmp/` logs and the agents' transcripts were all there afterwards
and the transcripts were snapshotted at the next Stop; and the `wip/` branches
held every milestone pushed before the restart — R1's two failing tests with
their recorded failure (23:12) and its fix with the recorded pass (23:21), R2's
failing test with its recorded failure (23:12). The batch was relaunched at
23:28 (run `wf_aabc0cb2-d31`) from the same base, and the shared prefix gained
a clause telling a worker whose branch already carries commits to read them
and continue, verifying rather than redoing. The relaunched batch landed at 03:22, so the
restart cost 25 minutes of two workers and nothing else.

Two properties of the harness, learned here: a `Workflow` run does not survive
a VM restart even when the session does — its agents are gone, the harness
lists them as stopped, and `resumeFromRunId` holds nothing for an agent that
never finished, so the answer is a relaunch; and a `send_later` reminder is
server-side and does survive, so it is deleted or re-armed to fit the relaunch.

content.content:
**Worktree state that is never committed.** The first repair batch forbade its
workers to commit, so that the gather could compose one clean commit per rung;
when the container died every worktree was dirty and four agents' work went
with it. The transcript backup does not cover this: it copies JSONL, not trees,
and it fires only at the main session's Stop. The fix is in the workflow design
(`batched-climb-plan.md` §3, revised 2026-09-18): each worker's worktree is on
its own `wip/<slug>` branch, pushed at every milestone, and the gather composes
from the branch's net change instead of the dirty tree. Two rules follow for
any long run: nothing that takes hours lives only on disk, and the coordinator
takes a turn every half hour or so (`send_later`) so that the Stop hook fires
and the agents' transcripts are snapshotted while they run.

input.message:
**Result:** 20 entries existed only in git. They are now in `POSITIONS-history.md`. One standing method had no home: the 45-minute check-in while a batch runs. It now has one.

Commit `2b1e4ea16` on branch `positions-audit`, worktree `/home/user/fortress-audit`, not pushed. It has the exact footer. `/home/user/fortress` was not touched and its status is clean.

## Step 1: nothing only in git

The two baselines hold 124 distinct entries. On `main`, 20 of them were in neither file. All 20 were lost in the first pass (`892687076`). The second pass lost nothing: every entry of the first pass's output is in one of the two files.

- **Removed whole (7):** the 09-24 "Stop the workers"; the 09-25 relaunch of the size probes; the 09-26 S2 probes go; the Fable reviews of batch 5's and batch 6's manifests; the answer-7 preparation go; the 23:37 45-minute check-ins.
- **Removed as remarks the protocol carries (2):** 01:08 no progress chat; 01:10 his words written once.
- **A go dropped from the entry (6):** 09-22 row 321 ("Prep please" and the `FnNameInfo` shadow); 09-23 rung P (the Fable synthesis); 09-26 judge tier (the Fable review of batch 4's manifest); the plan (W1 to W4); the second batch-5 answer ("Update protocol"); Astra's review (the row-388 probe and the Fable judgement).
- **Rewritten in place (5):** 09-20 check-in times; 09-23 time in chat; 09-24 POPL 2019; 09-26 the lineage note; 09-26 the size descriptor.

Each went in verbatim, in date order, with a comment like `<!-- 2026-09-27, first cleanup, 892687076: ... -->`. Where the history already held the first pass's shortened text, the older version sits just before it and its comment says "the next entry is what it left". The header gained one sentence saying what a first-cleanup comment means. The 01:10 entry went in as its last good text ("utterances").

The check script (scratchpad `audit/check.py`) treats an entry as a top-level `- ` bullet plus its indented lines. For each distinct entry of `e5414f5bf` and `892687076^`, it counts it as found in a file when the text equals an entry there ("exact") or appears whole inside one ("contained"). It fails unless the entry is found in exactly one of the two files. Output at `positions-audit`:
```
note [POSITIONS (contained)] e5414f5bf / Decisions on record: '- 2026-09-20, on the two libraries and the order of the compiler work: ...'
baseline entries, distinct across e5414f5bf and 892687076^: 124
  POSITIONS (contained): 1
  POSITIONS (exact): 38
  history (exact): 85
OK: every baseline entry verbatim in exactly one of the two files
```
At `main` the same script reports `history (exact): 65`, `neither: 20`, `FAILURES: 20`.

## Step 2: standing methods without a home

I read every sentence in the history that `POSITIONS.md` no longer carries, from both passes, and checked each candidate against the eight files. One item had no home:

- **Text:** "Monitor run every 45 minutes to keep the main session cached an ready to launch next batch", with the technique found the same hour: a series of one-shot `send_later` check-ins armed together.
- **Date:** 2026-09-26, 23:37 UTC.
- **Where it was:** only in the removed entry. FACTS has the technique but not the cadence or the reason. `remote-container.md` said "every half hour or so", for the backup snapshots only.
- **Where it went:** the existing sentence on long runs in `remote-container.md`, now: "the coordinator takes a turn every 45 minutes, a series of `send_later` check-ins armed together (`FACTS.md` § The container), so that the Stop hook fires and the agents' transcripts are snapshotted while they run, and so that the session stays cached, ready to launch the next batch (Pavol, 2026-09-26 23:37 UTC, `POSITIONS-history.md`)."

Everything else already has a home:
- The manifest review for batches 4, 5 and 6, and workers drafting the manifest: the workflow manual, "Preparing a batch record".
- The 09-19 gate decisions and the judge ruling while the gate runs: the manual and `POSITIONS.md`.
- Container-death recovery: `remote-container.md`.
- Output that is already flaky is a ledger row, not a stop; a rung's small items go to the ledger: `POSITIONS.md` and the manual.
- The S1 form and how the unrevised draft is cited: `POSITIONS.md`.
- A brief that is given the question and not the coordinator's answer, and the coordinator protecting its own context: protocol principles 2 and 5.

The rest were one-off gos, answered questions or replaced decisions.

## Two follow-on edits
- The workflow manual's source for the review method was `git show e5414f5bf:... lines 150 and 171`. It now points to `POSITIONS-history.md`, where those two entries are.
- The history comments on the three manifest-review entries and the 45-minute entry now name where the method they held lives, not just "removed as a go".

## Judgement calls to check
- **Section headings.** In both baselines, everything from 09-22 on was appended under "How he wants to be spoken to". I placed the restored entries under the heading the history file already uses for their kind, which follows the first pass's layout. So 09-23 rung P and everything dated 09-24 or later sit under "Decisions on record". The 09-20 check-in, 09-23 time and 01:08 entries sit under "How he wants to be spoken to". Taken literally, "original heading" would put the 09-24-onward decisions under "How he wants to be spoken to".
- **The 09-20 two-libraries entry.** The second pass added a sentence to it in `POSITIONS.md` without moving the old text. The original is intact as the entry's opening, so I counted it as present and did not copy it to history, which would have written it twice.
- **"Contained" in both files.** The four entries where the first pass only cut a trailing go now appear whole in `POSITIONS.md` and inside the restored full text in the history. This is by design and is not in the baseline check.
- **45 minutes as standing.** I read it as a standing rule, not a batch-6 go, because of his general reason and his "You've used the 45min check-in before". I also replaced "half hour", which assumes 45 minutes serves the backup-snapshot reason as well.
- **Not listed:** the '.'-only healthy check-in. Protocol § 3 already says he hears nothing unless something is wrong, and '.' is only the form that takes.

I've sent the report to the coordinator. The audit is committed as `2b1e4ea16` on branch `positions-audit` in `/home/user/fortress-audit`. It is not pushed, and `/home/user/fortress` was not touched.

- **Step 1:** 20 entries existed only in git. All of them were lost in the first pass; the second pass lost nothing. Each is now in `POSITIONS-history.md` word for word, in date order, with a comment naming the first cleanup. The check script now passes: all 124 distinct entries of the two baselines are in exactly one of the two files. On `main` it fails, with 20 in neither.
- **Step 2:** only one standing method had nowhere to live: Pavol's check-in every 45 minutes while a batch runs, so the session stays cached and ready to launch the next batch (2026-09-26, 23:37 UTC). I added it to the existing sentence about long runs in `remote-container.md`, which had said "every half hour or so". Everything else was already stated in one of the eight files, or was a one-off go, an answered question or a replaced decision.
- **Two small follow-on edits:** the workflow manual now cites the manifest-review entries in `POSITIONS-history.md` instead of in git. The history comments on those entries, and on the 45-minute one, now say where the method each held lives.

The report asks the coordinator to check five judgement calls:
- **Section headings:** I put decisions dated 09-24 or later, and the 09-23 rung P entry, under "Decisions on record", which is how the history file already sorts them. Taken literally, their original heading was "How he wants to be spoken to", because entries from 09-22 on had been appended there.
- **The 09-20 two-libraries entry:** the second pass added a sentence to it without moving the old text. The original is still whole at the start of the entry, so I counted it as present and did not copy it.
- **Four entries whose first-pass text now also sits in the history:** where the first pass only cut a trailing go, `POSITIONS.md` keeps the shortened entry and the history now holds the full original around it. The two baselines are unaffected.
- **The 45-minute cadence:** I read it as standing rather than a batch-6 go, from his general reason and "You've used the 45min check-in before".
- **The '.'-only healthy check-in:** I left it off the list, because protocol § 3 already says he hears nothing unless something is wrong.
